voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is the one who stood before the governor and was right. When an imperial judge offered our bishops chairs at Carthage, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and we stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one condemned by lawful authority and vindicated by God.

We confessed him as the creed confessed him, the Son, one God with the Father and the Spirit, who died and was raised. The quarrel was never about who he is. It was about whose hand may give what he gave to give. And he came to us as books. The codices a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry. We are the church that came out of that difference.

confidence.divergence_note: Assembled from a court transcript and from martyr texts, because those are the only places our own people speak at length about Christ - no christological or soteriological treatise of ours survives. The transcript is our own bishops' own words taken down by an imperial notary, which is unusually good ground; the printing it reaches this compilation through carries the worst OCR damage of any text in this corpus, so the wording is carried as reported sense and not as a quotable clause. That we confessed the same creed as our opponents is not our own claim but a finding all sides agree on: the division was called a schism, not a heresy, until Augustine's writing around 400 and the emperor's law of 405, and even then the charge rested on separation and not on any difference of creed.

voice_event.text:
He died and was raised. We held that as plainly as the church we fought held it, in the same Latin words. Beyond that, what his death accomplished - whether he died to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins - nobody among us wrote down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing, whose hand may give what the church gives, and we never turned it toward how the cross saves.

What we kept nearest was not a doctrine of the atonement but the pattern his own death showed. Our martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm on the last night before he was thrown from a cliff - shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. A bishop writing to the people of Carthage about two put to death closed by urging them to hurry after the two, who were waiting for them. In those texts the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
Ecclesia. The church. There was no neutral word for it here. The word itself was the argument. Two whole rival bodies claimed it, town by town, bishop for bishop. We held that we were the true one, and that our rival's favour with the state settled nothing.

It came straight from the Greek, through Latin, and it meant the assembly - the called-out ones. But in our towns it named two buildings, two bishops, two complete hierarchies, and no article of faith separated them. So when a man said ecclesia, he was not naming an agreed thing everyone pointed to the same way. He was making a claim about which body was the real one. That is why we would not call our rival Catholic - it would have granted them the word church before the case was argued. The naming fight was the same fight as the sacramental one, seen from two sides.

glosses.translational_sense: 'Surely the bigger, established church was the real one?' -- that is the one move this claim refuses. Numerical size, imperial recognition and possession of the word 'catholic' are three things; being the body of Christ is a fourth, and none of the first three settles it. If recognition by the ruling power decided the question, there would have been no reason to stand apart.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
We believed Jesus is who he is because the creed said so, and we held that creed as firmly as our rival did. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we confessed it in the same Latin words. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about whose hand may give what he gave to give.

What made him nearest to us was not a worked-out teaching but what happened to us. We were the church condemned by the state and vindicated by our dead. So the Christ we carried was the one who stood before the governor, lost the case, and was right. When the imperial judge offered our bishops chairs at Carthage, our own bishop of Constantina refused them - since Christ our Lord did not avoid standing before the governor, how much less may we? Two hundred and seventy-nine of us stood for three days. That is not a doctrine. It is who he had to be, for us to be what we were.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
Marculus, one of our clergy, lived it to the end. He had already refused worldly advancement before persecution ever reached him. The account spends its whole length on the life he had chosen. The cliff is the last four days of it.

They held him four days at Novapetra before they killed him. On the last night, after a day of fasting, he was shown a cup, a crown and a palm. The account reads them as a sight of what finishing would look like, not as a promise that dying was the goal. Before dawn they threw him from the cliff. The tradition says his body came down gently, and a bright cloud showed the brethren where he lay.

What the text praises is a man who was already what he was before anyone came for him. His death made that visible. We read his account aloud every year, at the grave, on the day he died.

voice_event.speaker: don
voice_event.text:
That we were not steady about what we said we were. We said a sacrament from a broken line is nothing, and must be given again, without exception. Then our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and afterwards took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We did not hide this. It sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its hardest.

And not every hand that went under our water chose to be there. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. Many of our own people did not want the water repeated at all. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

So yes, you could come back to us. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

confidence.divergence_note: The entry rite and the discipline questions are Documented and the record is unusually strong on both, because both are exactly what our opponents argued about at length. Prayer, the meal and fasting are much weaker and are marked so in the text itself: the eucharist reaches this telling through one hostile anecdote about a woman and a chalice, prayer through one account of a gathering being broken up, and fasting through a single martyr's fast before execution, which is not evidence of a communal rule. No liturgical text of ours survives, and no account of what undergoing the washing was like survives from anyone who underwent it. Whether entry was ever compelled rather than chosen is named here at the same level of generality `don.limit.bagai-violence-no-account` already uses for this world's hardest charges - it does not repeat that record's own specific, dated, hostile-only allegation, only cross-references it, because Doc_09 SS8 item 3 deliberately declined to narrate that allegation's particulars anywhere in this world's build and this record follows that same choice rather than reopening it. What this record does add directly is two pieces that are not hostile-only report: Augustine's own polemic conceding that almost all our laity found rebaptism distasteful, and a Donatist bishop's own recorded words at the 411 Conference. That transcript is itself extremely poor OCR (this corpus's worst, per `don.core.donatism` caution 2) and the rendering here is this record's own translation, not a certified one; re-read closely, the bishop's own answer reads as a claim to his own standing more than a plea in mitigation, and on either reading it names fear, in his own word, as what secured the ground.
